Power & utilities · Uganda

Transmission wayleaves in Uganda: structures, vegetation and new corridors

Keeping a wayleave clear means knowing what is inside it today and what has appeared since the last survey. We map structures and tall vegetation band by band along your transmission and distribution lines, date every feature, and flag the segments your wayleave teams should visit first. A person reviews every result.

Send your line for a proposal See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Wayleaves are paid for once and kept clear for decades

Uganda’s grid keeps growing, and new lines and interconnectors are being prepared. Each wayleave has to stay free of structures and tall vegetation long after compensation is paid.

“There is a new house under the line.”

A structure inside a wayleave is a safety risk and, the longer it stands, a harder conversation. The date it first appeared on imagery tells your team whether it predates the wayleave.

“The trees are growing back.”

On a line like the new 400 kV interconnector, vegetation and crops in the wayleave must not exceed 2 m, and they grow back between clearing cycles. A map of where tall vegetation stands tells the clearing crews where to go.

“We need the corridor for a new line.”

Before a new line’s route is fixed, the land it would affect can be counted option by option, and after it is fixed a dated baseline records what stood in the corridor.

“Towers have been damaged.”

New tracks, excavations and structures near tower bases show at the surface. Imagery cannot see theft, but it can show where the ground around towers has changed.

UETCL’s Grid Development Plan 2025–2040 records that “acquisition of way leaves for construction of transmission lines continues to be a challenge”, and lists “rampant vandalism” alongside it. Wayleave cases also reach the High Court. A dated record of what stood where does not settle a dispute; it gives the utility, the land team and the occupants the same facts.

Who this is for

  • Wayleave and land officers
  • Line maintenance and vegetation teams
  • Project teams for new lines and interconnectors
  • Resettlement and E&S teams
  • Demarcation and titling contractors
  • GIS and asset-records teams

The rules

A right of use in law; the width in each project’s framework

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

The Electricity Act

A licensee may place lines “over, along, across, or upon any land”, with a right of use and “prompt, fair, and adequate compensation” (s.67). Disputes go through the Land Act and Land Acquisition Act procedures (s.70), and land is compulsorily acquired where more than a right of use is needed (s.71). This is how UETCL’s resettlement framework summarises the Electricity Act (Cap. 145; Cap. 157 on ULII). No statutory wayleave width was found.

The Electricity (Amendment) Act 2022, assented to on 16 May 2022, added offences for cutting, removing, storing or moving supply lines or material without consent, and for receiving them, and raised the penalties for other offences.

A 60 m corridor on a new 400 kV line

UETCL’s resettlement policy framework for a new 400 kV interconnector (29 January 2026, Table 3.1) sets a 60 m corridor:

  • a 10 m right of way, acquired outright, with ownership passing to UETCL;
  • 25 m of wayleave on each side, where the owner keeps the land and the wayleave is registered as an easement and compensated;
  • in the wayleave, “No construction of permanent or temporary structures”, and “Vegetation and crops must not exceed 2 meters in height”.

UETCL commits to “ongoing monitoring and enforcement of land use restrictions”. The corridor is specific to that project; other lines follow their own frameworks.

Structures in the wayleave

A register, band by band, and what changed since the last survey

We buffer the line in its UTM zone, list each structure the review confirms with its distance to the centreline and its band (right of way, wayleave, or outside), and cut the line into 500 m stretches rated for encroachment density: high where more than five structures stand inside the widest band, medium for one to five, low for none. It is a count that tells your wayleave team where to go first, not a safety rating.

Re-surveys on a schedule you agree with us flag new and removed structures between dated surveys, automatically and then confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views and a change notice after each survey. Where a structure’s date matters, the imagery history of that spot shows roughly when it first appeared.

What you receive

  • A structure register: ID, distance to the line, band, chainage and coordinates
  • An encroachment-density rating for each 500 m stretch
  • New and removed structures between surveys
  • Tall vegetation inside the wayleave, by stretch
  • New tracks and excavations near tower bases
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, Shapefile, GeoJSON and KMZ layers

Vegetation

Where the 2 m rule is under pressure

Tall vegetation in the wayleave

Where tall vegetation stands inside the wayleave, mapped from drone elevation models and open canopy-height data. It is not a measured conductor clearance; drone surveys give the current picture where open data is older.

Clearing and regrowth

Where vegetation has been cleared, has regrown or has changed along the wayleave between dates, so clearing cycles go first to the stretches that need them.

Fire near the line

Notices of satellite-detected fire hotspots near your lines, and maps of the burnt area afterwards.

New lines and interconnectors

Route options, baselines, demarcation and titling

Route options

Structure counts, band by band, along alternative alignments for a new line or interconnector, so the land affected by each option can be weighed before the route is fixed.

Read

A dated baseline

A register of the structures in the corridor on dated imagery, to support the census, the valuation and the cut-off-date record under the Land Acquisition Act and the lender’s standards.

Read

Demarcation and titling support

As a subcontractor to the demarcation or titling contractor: the dated structure layer along the pegged corridor, the imagery history of each stretch, and GIS files that load into the surveyor’s system. The registered surveyor sets the boundaries.

Your own imagery

Analysis of the drone data your teams already capture

Some utilities capture their own corridor imagery. Send the orthophotos and elevation models your teams or contractors fly, and we run the same structure, vegetation and change analysis on them, with a structure detector tuned to your imagery and to local building styles where the default one is not enough, checked on part of your area first.

The same register format covers satellite and drone-derived results, so each line has one record however it was captured.

Drone flights along lines

Regulation 43(2)(b) of S.I. 96 of 2022 names “high tension cables and communication masts”, so any flight along or around them needs UCAA’s specific permission, on top of the approval and CDF security clearance each operation needs. Substations we treat as strategic installations.

Honest scope

What this is, and what it is not

What it supports

  • Wayleave enforcement and community engagement, with dated facts
  • Clearing plans, with the stretches where tall vegetation stands
  • Route selection and cut-off records for new lines
  • Demarcation and titling teams, as a subcontractor

What it does not do

  • Detect theft, vandalism or conductor faults
  • Measure conductor clearance or line sag
  • Decide whether a structure is authorised or compensated
  • Replace a cadastral survey or the registered surveyor

Frequently asked questions

Is there one statutory wayleave width in Uganda?

No statutory width was found. The Electricity Act gives a licensee a right of use over land with compensation, and the width comes from each project’s own framework, such as the 60 m corridor in UETCL’s January 2026 resettlement framework for a new 400 kV interconnector. Send us the widths that apply to your line, by voltage or by project.

Can you measure tree height under the line?

We map where tall vegetation stands inside the wayleave from drone elevation models and open canopy-height data. It is not a measured clearance to the conductors, and open canopy-height data is older in places, so a drone survey gives the current picture where the approvals allow one.

Can you detect tower vandalism or cable theft?

No. Satellites cannot see theft or vandalism. We flag new tracks, fresh excavations and new structures near tower bases between dated surveys, so patrols know where to look first.

Can you support wayleave demarcation or titling?

As a subcontractor to your surveyor or contractor, yes. We provide the dated structure and land-change layer along the pegged corridor and the documented imagery history of each stretch. Boundaries and titles come from the registered surveyor; our work is not a cadastral survey.

We fly our own drones along the lines. Can you use that imagery?

Yes. Send the orthophotos and elevation models your teams already capture and we run the same structure, vegetation and change analysis on them, with a structure detector tuned to your imagery where the default one is not enough.

Can a drone fly along our lines?

Only with UCAA’s specific permission, because regulation 43(2)(b) of S.I. 96 of 2022 names high tension cables, on top of the approval and CDF security clearance each operation needs. Satellite mapping needs none of that.

Send us your line

The line route or tower coordinates (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the voltage, the districts it crosses and the wayleave widths that apply. Tell us whether you need structures, vegetation or both, and we reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
